passages.happening:
Joab sees that the king's heart longs for Absalom. He sends to Tekoa for a wise woman and tells her to dress as a woman long in mourning, without oil on her skin, and to go to the king with words he gives her (verses 1-3).

She falls before the king: “Help me, O king!” (verse 4). She says she is a widow with two sons. They fought in the field with no one to separate them, and one killed the other. Now the whole clan demands the one who is left, to put him to death for his brother. ‘So they would extinguish my one remaining ember by not preserving my husband’s name or posterity on the earth’ (verse 7).

David promises to give orders for her. She presses him to swear by the LORD to stop the avenger of blood. “As surely as the LORD lives,” he vowed, “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 ended with Absalom in exile in Geshur and David longing for him. This chapter brings Absalom home, but only halfway.

Tekoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem, later known as the home of the prophet Amos. Joab, David's nephew and commander, is once again the man working behind the scenes, as he was when Uriah died. His motives are not stated. He may have seen that the king's paralysis over Absalom was harming the kingdom, since Absalom was now the likely heir, or he may have been placing himself well with the future king.

Two customs stand behind the woman's story. The first is blood vengeance. The nearest male relative of a murdered person had the duty to avenge his death, and the law called him the avenger of blood. The second is the family line. If her last son were killed, her husband's name would vanish and his land would pass out of the family. Her picture of her son as her one remaining ember, the last coal in a dying fire, captures that fear. As the highest judge, the king could step in to protect him.

Wise women appear elsewhere in Samuel; another saves her town in chapter 20. They seem to have been respected figures whose counsel and skill with words could shape events. Going without oil on the skin and hair was a sign of mourning in a dry land where oil was part of daily care.
passages.later:
The law named the avenger of blood and gave him his duty: ‘The avenger of blood is to put the murderer to death’ (Numbers 35:19). It also set up cities of refuge to protect anyone who had killed by accident (Numbers 35; Deuteronomy 19).

Tekoa is remembered as Amos's town: ‘These are the words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa’ (Amos 1:1).
passages.asks: Joab used a sad story to move the king. Ask when persuasion is wise and when it becomes manipulation. And ask whether you have ever let a story move you past a question you should have asked.

passages.t: The ruling turned on the king
passages.happening:
Then the woman asks leave to speak once more. “Why have you devised a thing like this against the people of God? When the king says this, does he not convict himself, since he has not brought back his own banished son? For surely we will die and be like water poured out on the ground, which cannot be recovered. Yet God does not take away a life; but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him” (verses 13-14).

The king asks her plainly, “Is the hand of Joab behind all this?” (verse 19). She admits it. David tells Joab to bring Absalom back, and Joab brings him from Geshur to Jerusalem. But the king adds, “He may return to his house, but he must not see my face” (verse 24). So Absalom goes to his own house, and he does not see the king.
passages.hearers:
The woman's appeal works like Nathan's parable in chapter 12. A made-up case draws the king into a ruling, and then the ruling is turned back on him. The echo is deliberate. But the two cases differ sharply. Nathan confronted David with his sin. This woman persuades him to overlook one.

Her speech moves from flattery to theology and back again. Its center is one of the most striking sentences in the historical books: God devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from him. The word for banished is used elsewhere of sheep scattered from the flock and of Israel driven into exile. She speaks it to serve Joab's plan, and yet it expresses a true longing, that God finds a way to bring exiles home.

Then David does a strange half-thing. He lets Absalom back into Jerusalem, and he will not see his face. Absalom has murdered his brother, and nothing is said of justice or of repentance. David longed for his son at the start of the chapter. Now that his son is near, he keeps him away.
passages.later:
The word for banished is the word the prophets use for God's scattered flock: ‘I will seek the lost, bring back the strays’ (Ezekiel 34:16). And the law promised the exiles of Israel, ‘Even if you have been banished to the farthest horizon, He will gather you and return you from there’ (Deuteronomy 30:4).

The law also set a limit the woman's story steps around: ‘You are not to accept a ransom for the life of a murderer who deserves to die’ (Numbers 35:31).
passages.hard:
Was David right to bring Absalom back?

Interpreters differ. Some see mercy: a father's love overcoming the demand for justice, and the woman's appeal to God's own wish to bring back the banished. Others see a failure of justice. Absalom had committed murder, showed no repentance, and was never held to account. On this reading David's decision was driven by longing, not right judgment, and the law did not allow a ransom for a murderer.

The narrator leaves clues that the second reading is closer to the text's view. The woman's case is invented and meant to move him, David's response is half-hearted, and Absalom's return leads straight to revolt. Yet the chapter does not condemn the wish for reconciliation itself. The trouble is not that David wanted his son back. It is that neither justice nor real repentance was any part of the return.
passages.asks: David brought his son home and would not look at him. Ask whether there is a reconciliation in your own life that stopped halfway. And ask what justice, or repentance, it is still waiting for.

passages.t: Absalom's beauty, a burning field, and a kiss
passages.happening:
‘Now there was not a man in all Israel as handsome and highly praised as Absalom’ (verse 25). From the sole of his foot to the top of his head he had no flaw. He cut his hair once a year, and it weighed two hundred shekels by the royal standard. Three sons were born to him, and a daughter named Tamar, ‘who was a beautiful woman’ (verse 27).

For two years Absalom lives in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face. He sends for Joab twice, and Joab will not come. So Absalom has his servants set Joab's barley field on fire. Joab comes at once (verses 28-31).

Absalom tells him to go to the king: ‘So now, let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me’ (verse 32). Joab tells the king, and David summons Absalom. He comes and bows facedown before the king. ‘Then the king kissed Absalom’ (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The narrator pauses to describe Absalom, which he rarely does with anyone. Physical description in these stories usually serves the plot, and this does. Absalom is handsome, praised and flawless to look at. A yearly haircut of two hundred shekels would be more than two kilograms if the shekel was eleven or twelve grams, though the value of the royal shekel is uncertain.

He names his daughter after his wronged sister, Tamar. The note that he had three sons sits uneasily with 18:18, where he says he has no son to carry on his name. Many interpreters conclude that the sons died young, which would also explain why they are not named.

The phrase about seeing the king's face comes again and again (verses 24, 28 and 32), building to the end of the chapter. Absalom gets his way by force: he burns a field to get a meeting. His words to the king sound like submission, but he never says he did wrong.

The chapter closes with a kiss and no recorded words. A kiss could mean welcome, reconciliation, or homage. Here it looks like reconciliation without any real reckoning, and the very next chapter shows Absalom using his freedom to steal the hearts of Israel.
passages.later: Chronicles names a daughter of Absalom in the royal house of the next generation. Solomon's son Rehoboam ‘married Maacah daughter of Absalom’ (2 Chronicles 11:20).
passages.asks: Absalom set a field on fire to get what he wanted. Ask whether you have ever forced someone's hand instead of facing the wrong between you. And ask what an honest conversation would have cost, and what it might have saved.
